shraddhanjali.sub: A quiet, simple way to inform relatives and friends about a loved one's passing and the prayer meeting, with a photo and a few respectful words.
shraddhanjali.article:
What is a shraddhanjali card?

When someone in the family passes away, the days that follow are heavy and full of small tasks. One of those tasks is letting relatives, neighbours, colleagues and old friends know what has happened and when they can come to offer their prayers. In the past this was done through phone calls, a notice in the local newspaper, or a printed card sent through the community. Today most families share a simple digital card on WhatsApp.

A shraddhanjali card is a tribute card. It usually carries a photo of the departed, their full name, the dates of birth and passing, a short line of prayer or remembrance, and the details of the prayer meeting. It is not decorative in the way a festival card is. Its purpose is to inform people clearly and to honour the person with dignity.

The same card is often called a besnu card in Gujarat, a prarthana sabha card or shok sabha card in many North Indian families, or simply an Om Shanti card. Whatever the name, the aim is the same: to gather people in prayer for the peace of the soul and to support the grieving family.

Customs after a death: a gentle overview

Customs after a death differ a great deal from one community, caste, region and even one family to another. What is described below is a general picture only. Elders in your family or your community priest will know what is followed in your home, and their guidance should always come first.

Besnu (Gujarat)

In many Gujarati families, the besnu is the gathering where relatives and friends come to sit with the family, offer condolences and join in prayer or bhajans. It is usually held within a few days of the death, often in the afternoon or evening, at home, at a community hall (wadi) or a temple. The besnu card tells people the date, time and place, and sometimes mentions whether it is for both ladies and gents together.

Uthamnu or Uthamna

The uthamnu (also written uthamna) is a prayer meeting held in many Gujarati and some Marwari families, commonly on the third day. In several communities the besnu and uthamnu are combined into a single prayer meeting, and the card simply says "Besnu and Uthamnu". In North India, a similar gathering is known as uthala or uthavna, where relatives gather, prayers are read, and the family is supported through the early days of grief.

Prarthana sabha or shok sabha

The prarthana sabha (prayer meeting) or shok sabha (condolence meeting) is common across North India and in many urban families everywhere. A photo of the departed is placed with a garland and a lamp, bhajans or the Gita path may be recited, and visitors offer flowers and fold their hands in silent prayer. Many families now keep only a prarthana sabha in place of several separate rituals, especially in cities.

Panidhol

In some Gujarati communities, panidhol is a ritual observed by the family, generally around the time of the besnu or uthamnu, marking the end of the first phase of mourning. The details vary widely, so families usually mention it on the card only if relatives are expected to attend.

Barmu and terahvi

The barmu (twelfth day) in Gujarat and the terahvi (thirteenth day) in North India mark the completion of the main mourning period. Rituals are performed for the peace of the soul, and in many families a meal is offered to Brahmins, relatives and the community. Some families invite close relatives only, while others invite a wider circle.

Pagdi rasam

In many North Indian families, the pagdi rasam is held on or near the terahvi. A turban is tied on the eldest son or the next head of the family in front of relatives, symbolising that he now carries the responsibilities of the household. It is a moment of both grief and continuity, and it is often mentioned on the same card as the terahvi.

Please remember that none of these customs is compulsory in one fixed form. Some families hold all of them, some only one, and many modern families announce a single prayer meeting and request that no other rituals be expected. All of these choices are respectful.

What to write in a condolence message

When you receive a shraddhanjali card, you may want to reply to the family or post a message in the group. A few simple words, written sincerely, mean far more than a long paragraph.

  • Keep it short. "Om Shanti. Deepest condolences to the family" is enough for most situations.
  • Use the person's name. Mentioning "Rameshbhai" or "Dadi ji" makes the message personal.
  • Share a small memory if you have one, such as their kindness, humour or the way they welcomed guests.
  • Offer help simply, for example with food, errands or picking up relatives from the station, and mean it.
  • Pray for strength for the family, not only for the peace of the soul.

There are also things best avoided:

  • Do not ask about the cause of death or the medical details in the group or in the first message.
  • Avoid phrases like "everything happens for a reason" or "at least they lived a long life", which can hurt even when kindly meant.
  • Do not use emojis, stickers or forwarded images with loud colours. A plain text message is more respectful.
  • Do not turn the conversation towards your own losses or problems.

Sharing on WhatsApp: simple etiquette

Sharing a prayer meeting card on WhatsApp has become normal and is widely accepted. A few thoughtful habits make it easier for everyone.

  1. Let one person share first. Usually a son, daughter, nephew or close family friend shares the card, and others forward it to their circles.
  2. Add a short line with the card, such as "With deep sorrow we inform you of the passing of our father. Prayer meeting details are in the card."
  3. Double-check dates and the venue before sending. Correcting a mistake later causes confusion at a difficult time.
  4. Do not expect replies to every message. The family may not be able to respond, and that is understood.
  5. If you are a visitor, reply in the group only once, and send personal messages directly to the family member you know.

How to make a shraddhanjali card on this site

The card maker on this page is designed to be calm and simple. You do not need any design skills, and nothing needs to be installed.

  1. Choose the type of card, such as Shraddhanjali, Besnu, Uthamna, Prarthana Sabha or Terahvi. The heading on the card changes accordingly.
  2. Add a photo of the departed. A clear, front-facing photo with a plain background works best.
  3. Enter the name as the family wishes it to appear, for example "Late Shri Rameshbhai Patel" or "Swargiya Smt. Kamla Devi Sharma".
  4. Add the dates of birth and passing, if the family wishes to show them.
  5. Fill in the prayer meeting details: date, time and venue.
  6. Add the family names under "In grief", such as sons, daughters, grandchildren or the whole family surname.
  7. Pick a tribute line from the suggested words, or write your own in a few simple sentences.
  8. Use the note line for anything extra, such as a contact number or "Only prayer meeting; no other rituals".
  9. Preview, download and share the card on WhatsApp or print it if needed.

Take a moment to read the card once more before sending, ideally with another family member. We hope this small tool makes one part of a painful time a little easier. May the departed soul rest in peace. Om Shanti.

faq.q: What is the difference between besnu and uthamnu?
faq.a: In many Gujarati families, the besnu is the gathering where people come to offer condolences and pray with the family, while the uthamnu is a prayer meeting usually held on the third day. Many communities now combine both into one meeting. Follow the practice of your family and community.

faq.q: Is it okay to share a prayer meeting card on WhatsApp?
faq.a: Yes. Sharing a digital prayer meeting card on WhatsApp is now common and accepted in most families. Add a short respectful line with the card and check all details carefully before sending.

faq.q: What should be written on a shraddhanjali card?
faq.a: Usually the photo and full name of the departed, dates of birth and passing, a short tribute or prayer line, the prayer meeting date, time and venue, and the names of the grieving family members. A contact number or a note about rituals can be added if needed.

faq.q: How do I reply to a condolence card or message?
faq.a: A short sincere message is best, such as: Om Shanti. Deepest condolences to the family. May God give you strength. Avoid emojis and do not ask about the cause of death in the first message.

faq.q: What is terahvi and pagdi rasam?
faq.a: Terahvi is the ritual on the thirteenth day after death, observed in many North Indian families to complete the main mourning period. Pagdi rasam, often held on the same day, is when a turban is tied on the eldest son or next head of the family in the presence of relatives.

faq.q: Can I write my own words on the card?
faq.a: Yes. You can choose one of the suggested tribute lines or type your own. Keep it simple and sincere, and if possible read it once with another family member before sharing.

invitations.article:
Why digital invitations have become so popular

A few years ago, inviting people to a family function meant printing cards, writing addresses by hand and visiting relatives one by one. That personal visit still has its place, especially for elders and close family. But for most occasions today, a clear and good-looking digital invitation sent on WhatsApp does the job beautifully. It reaches everyone on the same day, costs nothing to print, and the guest always has the date, time and venue saved on their phone.

Digital cards also make last-minute changes easy. If the venue shifts or the time changes, you can simply make a fresh card and send it again, instead of reprinting hundreds of copies.

Occasions you can make cards for

This section of the site has ready card makers for the most common family functions in Gujarat and North India:

  • Wedding invitations with Ganesh blessing, groom and bride names, and family details.
  • Engagement or ring ceremony (sagai, chandlo matli) invitations.
  • Birthday party invitations for children, parents and grandparents.
  • Griha pravesh or housewarming (vastu puja) invitations.
  • Baby shower invitations for godh bharai, seemant or srimant.
  • Naming ceremony (namkaran) invitations to welcome a newborn.
  • Puja invitations for Satyanarayan katha, havan, jagran and other religious gatherings.
  • Shop or office opening invitations for inauguration and muhurat.

What every good invitation should have

Whatever the occasion, a guest should be able to understand the card in a few seconds. Make sure it clearly shows:

  1. The occasion, written as a heading.
  2. Whose function it is, such as the couple, the child or the shop name.
  3. Date and day, for example "Sunday, 15 November 2026".
  4. Time, including separate timings for puja and meals if needed.
  5. Venue, with the area and city so that people can find it easily.
  6. Who is inviting, usually the family name or the hosts.

Optional extras include an RSVP number, a dress code, a note like "Lunch will follow the puja", or a short blessing line at the top.

How the card maker works

Open the page for your occasion and you will find a card with a suitable heading and design already set. Fill in the names, date, time and venue. Choose one of the suggested invitation lines or type your own. You can then download the card as an image and share it directly on WhatsApp, Instagram or any other app. Nothing needs to be installed, and you do not need an account.

Each occasion page also has a long list of ready WhatsApp messages: formal invitations for elders, casual ones for friends, reminder messages for the day before, and thank-you notes to send after the function.

A few etiquette tips

For elders and very close relatives, a phone call along with the digital card is always appreciated. Send the card early enough for people to plan, and a gentle reminder a day or two before. Avoid sending the same card again and again in large groups. And after the event, a short thank-you message leaves everyone with a warm feeling.

faq.q: Are the invitation cards free to make?
faq.a: Yes. You can make, download and share invitation cards on this site for free, without creating an account.

faq.q: Can I send these cards on WhatsApp?

faq.q: Is a digital invitation considered polite for a wedding?
faq.a: For most guests, yes. For elders and very close family, many people still prefer to call personally or deliver a printed card along with the digital one.

faq.q: How early should I send a digital invitation?
faq.a: About three to four weeks ahead for weddings, one to two weeks for most other functions, and a reminder one or two days before the event.

wedding.article:
The wedding card sets the tone

In Indian families, the wedding invitation is the first real announcement of the celebration. Traditionally the first card is placed before Lord Ganesh or the family deity, and only then are the rest sent out. Even today, when many invitations travel by WhatsApp, families take great care with the wording, the names and the order in which relatives are mentioned.

A digital wedding card does not replace the warmth of a personal visit to elders, but it makes sure every guest has the correct details on their phone, and it reaches relatives in other cities and abroad on the same day.

What to include in a wedding invitation

  • Blessing line at the top, such as "|| Shri Ganeshaya Namah ||" or the name of your kuldevi.
  • Names of the groom and bride, often with parents' names, for example "Chi. Rohan (son of Smt. and Shri Mahesh Shah)".
  • Date and day of the wedding, along with the muhurat or hast melap time if you wish.
  • Venue, with the name of the hall or party plot and the area.
  • Inviting family, usually the grandparents or parents, with the family surname.
  • RSVP or contact, and a note about the reception or other functions.

If you have several functions such as mehendi, haldi, sangeet, mandap muhurat and reception, you can either make one main card or a separate card for each function. Many families send the main card first and then a simple card for each event closer to the date.

Traditional wording versus modern wording

Traditional

Traditional cards speak on behalf of the elders and invite guests to bless the couple. A typical line is: "With the blessings of the Almighty and our elders, we cordially invite you and your family to grace the auspicious occasion of the marriage of our son." In Gujarati families, words like Chi. (Chiranjeevi) for the groom and Chi. Sau. Ka. for the bride are common, and North Indian cards often use Ayushman and Ayushmati.

Modern

Modern cards are often written in the voice of the couple and are warm and short: "Together with our families, we are getting married and would love for you to be there." These work well for friends, colleagues and younger relatives.

There is no rule that you must choose one style. Many families send a traditional card to relatives and a modern one to friends.

Sample format

|| Shri Ganeshaya Namah ||

Wedding Invitation. Chi. Rohan weds Chi. Sau. Ka. Priya. With the blessings of our elders, we request your gracious presence at the wedding ceremony on Sunday, 6 December 2026 at 7:00 PM, Shubh Party Plot, S.G. Highway, Ahmedabad. With best compliments from Smt. Nita and Shri Mahesh Shah and family.

When to send and how to remind

  1. Save the date: two to three months ahead, especially for destination weddings or guests who must travel.
  2. Main invitation: three to four weeks before the wedding.
  3. Function-wise cards: about a week before, with timings for each event.
  4. Reminder: one or two days before, with the venue location.
  5. Thank-you message: within a few days after the wedding.

Etiquette to keep in mind

Call elders and very close relatives personally before or along with sending the card. Send cards individually rather than in large groups wherever possible, as it feels more personal. Spell every name carefully, and ask a family member to check the card before sharing. If the wedding is only for close family, mention it gently so that no one feels confused. And never forget to invite the neighbours who help so much during the preparations.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Wrong or missing day: always write the day with the date, such as "Sunday, 6 December 2026". It helps people catch errors.
  • Confusing timings: if the wedding runs late into the night, write "Hast melap: 11:30 PM" and "Dinner: from 8:00 PM" separately so guests know when to arrive.
  • Too much text: a phone screen is small. Keep the main card short and send extra details, like hotel bookings or parking, as a separate message.
  • Forgetting the location: send a location pin with the card, especially for farmhouses and party plots outside the city.
  • Missing names of elders: in many families, grandparents are mentioned first as the inviting elders. Check with the family before finalising.

A message to send along with the card

A card alone can feel impersonal. Add a line or two of your own, such as: "Namaste Kaka and Kaki, with the blessings of the family, Rohan's wedding is fixed for 6 December. Please do come with the whole family. The card is attached, and Papa will also call you." For friends, something like "The big day is finally here! Please block 6 December, we will be waiting for you" works well. You will find many more ready messages in the list below this article.

Printed card and digital card together

Many families now print a small number of cards for elders, the family deity and very close relatives, and use the digital card for everyone else. This saves money and paper without losing the traditional feeling. If you do both, make sure the wording, dates and venue on the two cards match exactly.

How to make a wedding card on this site

  1. Enter the groom's name and the bride's name. They appear joined with "weds".
  2. Add the date, time and venue.
  3. Enter the inviting family's names under "With best compliments from".
  4. Pick an invitation line or write your own.
  5. Add an RSVP number or a short note if needed.
  6. Preview, download and share on WhatsApp.

You can make the card again as many times as you like, so feel free to create separate versions for relatives and friends.

faq.q: What should be written at the top of a Hindu wedding card?
faq.a: Most families begin with a blessing such as || Shri Ganeshaya Namah || or the name of their family deity. You can edit the top line on this card to match your tradition.

faq.q: How early should I send a wedding invitation?
faq.a: Send a save-the-date two to three months ahead if guests need to travel, the main invitation three to four weeks before, and a reminder one or two days before the wedding.

faq.q: Is it okay to invite relatives only on WhatsApp?
faq.a: For most guests a digital card is fine. For elders and very close relatives, it is polite to also call them personally or visit with a printed card.

faq.q: What do Chi. and Chi. Sau. Ka. mean on a Gujarati wedding card?
faq.a: Chi. stands for Chiranjeevi, a blessing for long life used before the groom's name. Chi. Sau. Ka. stands for Chiranjeevi Saubhagyakankshini, used before the bride's name.

faq.q: Can I make separate cards for mehendi, sangeet and reception?
faq.a: Yes. Make the main card first, then change the heading line, date, time and venue to create a card for each function.

faq.q: What should I send after the wedding?
faq.a: A short thank-you message to guests for their presence and blessings is a lovely gesture. You will find ready thank-you messages in the list on this page.

engagement.sub: Invite family and friends to the sagai, chandlo matli or ring ceremony with a neat digital card you can share on WhatsApp.
engagement.article:
The engagement: the first celebration of a new relation

The engagement is the moment two families formally accept each other and announce the coming wedding. In Gujarati families it is often called sagai or chandlo matli, where the bride's family applies a tilak to the groom and gifts are exchanged. In North India, the sagai, roka or ring ceremony is usually a lively gathering with the exchange of rings, sweets and blessings. Some families keep it very small with only close relatives, while others hold a full party.

Whatever the scale, a clear invitation helps guests arrive on time and know what to expect.

What to include

  • A top line such as "Ring Ceremony", "Sagai Samaroh" or a small blessing.
  • The names of both the boy and the girl, joined with "&".
  • Date, day and time of the ceremony, and the meal timing if there is a lunch or dinner.
  • Venue with area and city.
  • Inviting family names.
  • An optional note about dress code, RSVP or parking.

Traditional versus modern wording

Traditional

Traditional wording is usually written from the parents' side: "With the grace of God and blessings of our elders, we are pleased to invite you to the engagement ceremony of our son Chi. Karan with Chi. Sau. Ka. Neha." It is formal, respectful and suitable for elders and extended family.

Modern

Modern wording is lighter and often in the couple's own voice: "We said yes! Join us as we exchange rings and begin our forever." This is lovely for friends, cousins and colleagues.

Sample format

Ring Ceremony

Karan and Neha. With the blessings of our elders, we invite you to the engagement ceremony on Saturday, 14 November 2026 at 6:30 PM, followed by dinner, at Hotel Sapphire, Vadodara. With best compliments from the Mehta and Joshi families.

When to send and reminders

Engagements are sometimes planned quickly, so a card sent even ten to fifteen days ahead is perfectly fine. For a larger function, try to send it two to three weeks before. Send a short reminder with the location a day before, and a thank-you note after the ceremony. If the engagement is a close family affair, it is kind to send a simple announcement to wider relatives afterwards so no one feels left out.

Etiquette for engagement invitations

Both families usually invite their own relatives, so agree beforehand on the number of guests and the wording, especially if one common card is used. Make sure both family names are shown with equal respect. If the ceremony is private, mention "in the presence of close family" gently rather than leaving guests guessing. Personally call elders from both sides. Avoid posting the card on social media before both families are comfortable with the news being public.

It is also thoughtful to mention the dress theme if there is one, and to share a location pin with outstation guests. If there is a separate roka or tilak ritual in the morning and a party in the evening, list both timings clearly.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Unequal importance to both sides: if one family's name appears in large letters and the other's is missing, it can hurt feelings. Mention both families respectfully.
  • Unclear programme: if there is a puja or tilak before the ring exchange, write both timings so that elders come for the ritual and friends for the party.
  • No meal information: guests like to know whether dinner is served. A simple "Dinner to follow" solves this.
  • Forgetting outstation relatives: engagements are often fixed quickly. Call relatives from other cities as early as possible so that they can plan travel.

A message to send along with the card

For elders, a respectful note works well: "Jai Shri Krishna Masi, we are very happy to share that Karan's engagement with Neha is fixed. The ceremony is on 14 November in Vadodara. Please come and bless them. Card attached." For friends, you can be more playful: "It's official! Ring ceremony on 14 November. You have to be there!" The list below has many more options for every kind of guest.

Announcing the engagement afterwards

Not every relative can be invited to an engagement, especially if it is a small family function. After the ceremony, many families share a simple card or photo with a line like "With the blessings of our elders, Karan and Neha got engaged today. Please keep your blessings with them." This keeps everyone included and happy, and it is a gentle way to let the wider family know before the wedding invitations go out.

You can use the same card maker for this: change the wording to an announcement line and remove the date and venue fields.

Making the card on this site

  1. Type the boy's name and the girl's name. They will be joined with "&".
  2. Fill in the date, time and venue.
  3. Add the inviting family names.
  4. Choose an invitation line or write your own.
  5. Add a note if needed, such as "Dinner to follow".
  6. Preview, download and share.

You can quickly make a second version for friends with more casual wording. Once the engagement is done, the wedding card maker is only a click away when you are ready to announce the big day.

faq.q: What is chandlo matli?
faq.a: Chandlo matli is a Gujarati engagement ritual where the bride's family applies a tilak (chandlo) on the groom's forehead and gives a matli, a small pot or box with gifts and a coconut, to formalise the relationship.

faq.q: How early should I send an engagement invitation?
faq.a: Ten days to three weeks before is usually enough. Send a reminder with the location a day before the ceremony.

faq.q: Who sends the engagement invitation?
faq.a: Usually both families send cards to their own relatives and friends. Some families make one common card with both family names.

faq.q: Can I write the couple's names without parents' names?
faq.a: Yes. Modern cards often show just the couple's names. Parents' names can be added in the inviting family line.

faq.q: What is the difference between roka and engagement?
faq.a: Roka is a small ritual in many North Indian families where both sides formally agree to the match. The engagement or ring ceremony is usually a larger event where rings are exchanged.

faq.q: Is it okay to share the engagement card on social media?
faq.a: It is best to wait until both families are comfortable making the news public. Until then, share it only with invited guests.

birthday-party.article:
Birthdays in Indian families

Birthdays have become a much bigger family event than they used to be. A child's first birthday is often celebrated like a small function, with relatives, a theme, a cake and sometimes a puja in the morning. Milestone birthdays of parents and grandparents, such as the 50th, 60th (shashtipurti) or 75th (amrut mahotsav), are also celebrated with great love. And of course there are the simpler get-togethers at home with cousins and neighbours.

A small digital card makes all of these feel a little more special, and it helps guests remember the date, time and place.

What to include in a birthday invitation

  • Whose birthday it is, and the age if you want to mention it, such as "Aarav turns 1" or "Celebrating 60 years of Papa".
  • Date and day, and the start time. For kids' parties, an end time helps parents plan pick-ups.
  • Venue, whether home, society clubhouse, restaurant or banquet hall.
  • Hosts, usually parents for a child or children for a parent's birthday.
  • Theme or dress code, if any, like "Jungle theme" or "Wear something red".
  • RSVP number, especially if food is ordered per head.

Traditional versus modern wording

Traditional and formal

For elders' milestone birthdays, formal wording feels right: "With the blessings of God, we are celebrating the 75th birthday of our respected father. We request your presence to bless him on this joyful occasion." Some families combine the celebration with a Satyanarayan katha or a small havan in the morning.

Modern and playful

For children and friends, fun wording works best: "Balloons, cake and lots of fun! Come celebrate with Myra as she turns 5." Short lines and a playful tone suit a cheerful card.

Sample formats

Kids: You're invited! Birthday Party. Aarav is turning 1. Sunday, 8 November 2026, 5:00 PM to 8:00 PM, The Party Hall, Vesu, Surat. With love from Mummy and Papa.

Elders: Birthday Celebration. 60 glorious years of Shri Rajendra Agarwal. Saturday, 21 November 2026, 7:00 PM, Hotel Park Plaza, Jaipur. With love, his children and grandchildren.

When to send and reminders

For a home party, a week ahead is enough. For a bigger party at a venue, send the card two weeks before and ask people to confirm. A reminder the evening before or on the morning of the party is always useful, especially for children's parties, since parents juggle many plans. After the party, a short thank-you message with a nice photo is a warm way to close.

Etiquette tips

For children's parties, invite the whole class or a clear small group, so that no child feels left out. Mention if siblings are welcome. If you do not want gifts, write it gently, for example "Your blessings are the only gift we need". For a surprise party, remember to tell guests clearly that it is a surprise and to arrive before the birthday person. Keep the invitation in a separate chat or group so the surprise is not spoiled.

Consider food preferences too. Mention if the food is pure vegetarian or Jain, as many guests appreciate knowing in advance.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Only the date, no day: writing "Sunday, 8 November" instead of just "8/11" avoids confusion, especially between Indian and foreign date formats.
  • No end time for kids: parents need to know when to pick up their children.
  • Wrong spelling of the child's name: it happens more often than you think. Read the card once aloud before sharing.
  • Too many forwards: send the card once, and one reminder. Repeated forwards in the same group can annoy people.
  • Venue without landmark: for banquet halls and restaurants, add the area or a landmark so guests do not get lost.

A message to send along with the card

A short personal line makes the card warmer. For relatives: "Namaste Bua ji, Aarav's first birthday is on 8 November at 5 PM. Please come and bless him. Card attached." For school parents: "Hello! Myra is turning 5 and would love to have Riya at her party on Sunday from 4 to 7 PM. Please let me know if she can come." There are more ready messages in the list below.

Milestone birthdays of elders

When children plan a 60th, 70th or 75th birthday for their parents, the invitation often becomes a small tribute. You can add a line such as "Celebrating 75 years of love, strength and blessings" and invite old friends and colleagues of the birthday person, not only family. Some families collect short messages or photos from guests beforehand to make a memory book. Mention it on the card or in a separate message so people can send their wishes in time.

How to make a birthday card on this site

  1. Enter the birthday person's name, with age if you like, such as "Aarav turns 1".
  2. Add the date, time and venue.
  3. Enter the host names.
  4. Choose a fun or formal invitation line, or write your own.
  5. Use the note for theme, RSVP or "Return gifts for all kids".
  6. Download and share on WhatsApp.

Making a new version is easy, so you can have one card for family and another for your child's school friends.

faq.a: Shashtipurti is the celebration of completing 60 years of age. Many families mark it with a puja followed by a family gathering.

faq.a: It helps. Parents can plan pick-ups and other commitments more easily when they know when the party ends.

griha-pravesh.article:
Griha pravesh: stepping into a new home

Moving into a new home is one of the happiest milestones for any family. In Hindu tradition, the first entry into a new house is done with a griha pravesh ceremony on an auspicious muhurat. The lady of the house often enters first, sometimes kicking a kalash filled with rice, a Ganesh puja and vastu shanti puja are performed, and in many homes milk is boiled over in the new kitchen as a sign of abundance. In Gujarat the ceremony is often called vastu puja or vastu shanti, while in North India it is widely known as griha pravesh or grih pravesh puja.

After the puja, relatives and friends come to see the home, take prasad and share a meal. A clear invitation helps everyone reach at the right time, especially since the puja muhurat is fixed.

What to include

  • A blessing line such as "|| Shri Ganeshaya Namah ||" or "Shubh Griha Pravesh".
  • Family name, for example "Sharma Niwas" or "The Patel family".
  • Date and puja muhurat, and the time for lunch or dinner.
  • Full address of the new home, including society name, flat or bungalow number and a landmark.
  • Hosts and a contact number.
  • A note about parking, the lift or the location pin.

Traditional versus modern wording

Traditional

"With the blessings of Lord Ganesh and our elders, we have been blessed with a new home. We cordially invite you to the Griha Pravesh and Vastu Puja and request you to bless our family." This style suits relatives and elders.

Modern

"New address, same us! Come over for our housewarming and help us fill our new home with love and laughter." Friends and colleagues enjoy this lighter style.

Sample format

|| Shubh Griha Pravesh ||

Griha Pravesh. The Sharma family. We invite you to the vastu puja and griha pravesh of our new home on Thursday, 12 November 2026. Puja at 9:00 AM, lunch from 12:30 PM. Address: B-402, Shanti Residency, Near Sector 21 Market, Gurugram. With best compliments from Smt. Sunita and Shri Anil Sharma.

When to send and reminders

Once the muhurat is fixed, send the card about one to two weeks ahead. Because new homes can be hard to find, share a location pin along with the card, and send a reminder the day before with directions. On the day itself, a short message like "Puja has started, please come" helps late guests. Afterwards, a thank-you message with a photo of the family in front of the new home is a nice touch.

Etiquette for housewarming invitations

Invite your new neighbours too. It is a warm way to start your life in a new society. Mention whether the gathering is for the puja only or includes a meal, so guests can plan. If space is limited, you may invite close family for the puja and others for an evening get-together, with clear timings on separate cards. Guests traditionally bring a small gift for the new home, but it is never compulsory, and some hosts write "Your blessings are enough".

Remember that many elderly relatives prefer a phone call. A card on WhatsApp followed by a short call to the elders is a respectful combination.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Incomplete address: a new society may not show up on maps yet. Write the society name, wing, flat number and a well-known landmark.
  • Missing the muhurat time: the puja begins at a fixed time, so guests who wish to attend the puja must know it clearly.
  • No meal information: mention whether lunch or dinner is served, or only prasad.
  • Forgetting the society's rules: some buildings have limited parking or lift timings. A short note saves guests trouble.

A message to send along with the card

For relatives: "Namaste Mama ji, with God's grace we have bought our own home in Gurugram. The griha pravesh puja is on 12 November at 9 AM, followed by lunch. Please come with Mami ji and bless us. Card and location attached." For friends: "We finally moved! Housewarming on Saturday evening, come see the new place." More options are in the list below.

Griha pravesh for a rented home or renovated house

Many families also perform a small puja when moving into a rented flat or after a major renovation of the old home. The invitation can be simpler in such cases, often just for close family and neighbours. You can use the same card maker, change the heading line to "Vastu Puja" or "Satyanarayan Katha", and keep the wording short and warm.

If you are moving to a new city, a housewarming is also a lovely way to meet new neighbours. Leaving a printed copy of the card at the neighbouring doors, along with a small box of sweets, is a thoughtful gesture that is always remembered.

How to make it on this site

  1. Enter the family or house name, such as "Sharma Niwas".
  2. Add the date and puja time.
  3. Type the full address of the new home as the venue.
  4. Add the host names.
  5. Pick a traditional or modern line, or write your own.
  6. Use the note for lunch timing or a landmark, then download and share.

May your new home be filled with peace, health and prosperity.

faq.q: What is griha pravesh?
faq.a: Griha pravesh is the ceremony of entering a new home for the first time on an auspicious muhurat, usually with Ganesh puja and vastu puja, followed by a meal with family and friends.

faq.q: Is vastu puja the same as griha pravesh?
faq.a: They are closely linked. Vastu puja or vastu shanti is the puja done for the peace and harmony of the home, and it is usually performed as part of the griha pravesh ceremony.

faq.q: How early should I send a housewarming invitation?
faq.a: About one to two weeks before the muhurat, with a reminder and location pin a day before.

faq.q: Should I write the full address on the card?
faq.a: Yes. Include the society name, flat or house number and a landmark. Also send a location pin separately on WhatsApp.

faq.q: What gift do guests usually bring to a griha pravesh?
faq.a: Common gifts include a small idol, a plant, kitchen items, a photo frame or sweets. Gifts are optional, and blessings are what matter most.

faq.q: Can I invite some guests for the puja and others for dinner?
faq.a: Yes. Make two versions of the card with different timings, one for the puja and one for the evening gathering.

baby-shower.article:
Blessing the mother-to-be

In Indian families, the months of pregnancy are a time of care and blessings. Many communities hold a special ceremony, usually in the seventh or eighth month, to celebrate the mother-to-be and pray for a safe delivery and a healthy baby. In Gujarat it is called seemant or srimant (also kholo bharvo in some families), in North India it is widely known as godh bharai, and in other regions it may be called valaikappu, dohale jevan or saad. Today many families also call it a baby shower and add modern touches like games and a decorated photo corner.

During the ceremony, women of the family fill the lap of the mother-to-be with fruits, dry fruits, coconut, sweets and gifts, apply haldi-kumkum, put bangles on her wrists and give their blessings. It is a gentle, joyful occasion, and the invitation should feel the same way.

What to include

  • Name of the mother-to-be, for example "Sau. Riddhi Patel".
  • Name of the ceremony, such as Seemant, Godh Bharai or Baby Shower.
  • Date, day and time, including the meal timing.
  • Venue, whether home, a community hall or a banquet.
  • Hosts, often the in-laws or both families together.
  • A note, for example "Ladies only", "Dress code: pastel" or an RSVP number.

Traditional versus modern wording

Traditional

"With the blessings of the Almighty, we joyfully invite you to the seemant sanskar of our daughter-in-law Sau. Riddhi. Kindly come and bless the mother and the little one on the way." This style feels right for elders and relatives.

Modern

"A little one is on the way! Join us for a baby shower full of love, laughter and blessings for Riddhi." Friends and cousins will enjoy this cheerful tone.

Sample format

Baby Shower

Seemant Sanskar of Sau. Riddhi Patel. Sunday, 22 November 2026, 10:00 AM, followed by lunch. Venue: Patel Samaj Hall, Gandhinagar. With best compliments from Smt. Hansaben and Shri Kantilal Patel.

When to send and reminders

Since the ceremony date depends on the month of pregnancy and a good muhurat, cards are often sent about ten days to two weeks ahead. Send a reminder the day before. Because the mother-to-be should not be tired, it helps to mention a clear start and end time so the function stays relaxed. Afterwards, a short thank-you message on behalf of the mother-to-be is a lovely gesture.

Etiquette and sensitivity

Some families prefer to keep the pregnancy private until later, so check with the couple before sharing the card widely. Many traditional seemant and godh bharai ceremonies are mainly for women, while modern baby showers often include everyone; mention this clearly to avoid awkwardness. Avoid predicting or joking about whether the baby will be a boy or a girl on the card. Keep the wording gentle and positive.

If the ceremony is held at the mother's parental home or combined with a puja, mention that too. For outstation relatives, sending the card a little earlier helps them plan.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Sharing too early: check with the couple before posting the card in large groups or on social media.
  • Long functions: the mother-to-be tires easily. Plan a comfortable two or three hours and mention the timing.
  • Unclear guest list: if it is a ladies-only ceremony, say so kindly on the card.
  • No seating note: for a function at home, ask a few guests to come in shifts if space is limited.

A message to send along with the card

For elders: "Jai Shri Krishna Kaki, we are holding Riddhi's seemant on 22 November at 10 AM at the Samaj Hall. Please come and give her your blessings. Card attached." For friends: "It's baby shower time for Riddhi! Come for games, food and lots of love on Sunday morning." More ideas are in the list below this article.

When the ceremony is at the parental home

In many families, after the seemant or godh bharai, the mother-to-be goes to her parents' home for the delivery. Sometimes the ceremony itself is held there, hosted by her parents. In that case, the card can show both families as hosts, for example "With best compliments from the Patel and Shah families". This makes relatives from both sides feel equally welcome.

If some relatives cannot come, you can later send them a photo and a short thank-you message. They will be happy to feel included in the celebration and will send their blessings from afar.

How to make the card on this site

  1. Enter the name of the mother-to-be.
  2. Add the date, time and venue.
  3. Enter the hosts, such as the in-laws or both families.
  4. Choose a traditional or modern invitation line, or write your own.

faq.q: What is seemant or srimant?
faq.a: Seemant, also called srimant, is the Gujarati ceremony for a pregnant woman, usually in the seventh month, where elders bless her and pray for a safe delivery and a healthy baby.

faq.q: Is godh bharai the same as a baby shower?
faq.a: Godh bharai is the traditional North Indian ceremony of filling the lap of the mother-to-be with fruits, sweets and gifts. A baby shower is the modern name, and many families now combine both.

faq.q: In which month is godh bharai done?
faq.a: Most families hold it in the seventh or eighth month of pregnancy, on a date chosen by the elders or priest.

faq.q: Is a baby shower only for ladies?
faq.a: Traditional ceremonies are often mainly for women, but many modern baby showers include everyone. Mention it clearly on the card.

faq.q: How early should I send the invitation?
faq.a: About ten days to two weeks before, with a reminder one day before the ceremony.

faq.q: What should I avoid writing on a baby shower card?
faq.a: Avoid guessing or joking about whether the baby will be a boy or a girl. Keep the wording warm, gentle and positive.

naming-ceremony.article:
Namkaran: giving the baby a name

The namkaran sanskar is one of the traditional sixteen sanskars in Hindu life. It is the ceremony where the baby is formally given a name. Many families consult a priest who looks at the birth chart and suggests a starting letter, and the name is then chosen with love by the parents and grandparents. In several Gujarati families, the father's sister, the foi, has the special honour of naming the child, a custom known as foi nu naam. In North India, the chhathi on the sixth day and the namkaran around the eleventh or twelfth day are common, though many families now hold it on a convenient date within the first few months.

The ceremony is usually a small puja followed by the naming, blessings for the baby and a meal. Relatives look forward to meeting the newborn, and a nice invitation adds to the joy.

What to include

  • A top line such as "Welcome, little one" or "|| Shri Ganeshaya Namah ||".
  • Who is inviting: usually the baby's parents or grandparents. Since the name is not yet announced, the card often says "Baby of Pooja and Amit".
  • Date, day and time of the puja and the meal.
  • Venue, often the family home or a small hall.
  • An optional note, such as "Name to be announced at the ceremony" or an RSVP number.

Traditional versus modern wording

Traditional

"By the grace of God, we have been blessed with a baby boy. We cordially invite you to the namkaran sanskar and request you to bless our little one." This formal style is suitable for elders and relatives.

Modern

"Our little one is ready for a name! Join us as we reveal it and celebrate together." Friends love the sense of surprise in this style.

Sample format

Welcome, little one

Naming Ceremony. Baby of Pooja and Amit Verma. Sunday, 29 November 2026, puja at 11:00 AM followed by lunch, at our home, 12 Civil Lines, Kanpur. With love from Smt. Asha and Shri Suresh Verma (grandparents).

When to send and reminders

Because the namkaran date is often fixed by the priest a short time before, invitations are usually sent about a week in advance. A reminder the evening before is helpful. After the ceremony, share a photo of the baby with the new name and a thank-you message. Relatives who could not come will be happy to know the name.

Etiquette tips

New parents and the baby need rest, so keep the gathering at a comfortable size and the timings clear. Guests should be reminded gently not to visit if they are unwell. If the family follows the custom of the foi naming the baby, make sure she is informed first and has the details early. If you want to keep the name a surprise, do not print it on the card; simply write "Name reveal at the ceremony".

Also think about the baby's routine. Late-night functions can be tiring for a newborn, so a late-morning puja with lunch is a popular choice.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Revealing the name too early: if you want a surprise, do not print the name or mention it in the message.
  • Too many guests: a newborn is sensitive to crowds and noise. Invite the people who matter most.
  • Unclear timings: mention when the puja starts and when the meal is served.
  • Forgetting the foi: where the aunt names the baby, inform her personally before anyone else.

A message to send along with the card

For relatives: "Namaste Dadi ji, the namkaran of our little one is on 29 November at 11 AM at home. Please come and bless the baby. Card attached." For friends: "The little one is ready for a name! Small puja and lunch at home on Sunday. Would love to see you." You will find more messages in the list below.

Choosing a name and the role of the rashi

Many families ask the priest for the starting letter according to the baby's rashi or nakshatra. Others choose a name purely because they love its meaning or because it honours an elder. Both ways are common today. Some families announce two names: a rashi name used in rituals and a call name used daily. If you plan to do this, you can mention it in the thank-you message after the ceremony.

Whatever you choose, the namkaran is a moment for the whole family to welcome the child. The card is simply a warm way to bring everyone together for that moment.

How to make the card on this site

  1. Enter "Baby of" with the parents' names, or the baby's name if you are sharing it after the ceremony.
  2. Add the date, time and venue.
  3. Enter the host names, often parents or grandparents.
  4. Pick a traditional or modern line, or write your own.
  5. Add a note such as "Name reveal at the ceremony".
  6. Download and share on WhatsApp.

May your little one grow up healthy, happy and blessed.

faq.q: When is the namkaran ceremony done?
faq.a: Traditionally around the eleventh or twelfth day after birth, but many families now hold it on a convenient date within the first few months, as advised by the family priest.

faq.q: Who names the baby in Gujarati families?
faq.a: In many Gujarati families, the father's sister (foi) has the honour of naming the baby, a custom called foi nu naam. The name is usually decided together with the parents.

faq.q: What is chhathi?
faq.a: Chhathi is a ceremony held on the sixth day after birth in many North Indian families, with prayers to Chhathi Maiya for the baby's health and long life.

faq.q: What should I write on the card if the name is a surprise?
faq.a: Write Baby of followed by the parents' names, and add a note like Name reveal at the ceremony.

faq.q: How early should I send a naming ceremony invitation?
faq.a: About a week before is usual, with a reminder the evening before.

faq.q: Can I use this card to announce the baby's name afterwards?
faq.a: Yes. Enter the baby's name, change the wording to a thank-you or announcement line, and share it with relatives.

puja.sub: Invite relatives and neighbours to a Satyanarayan katha, havan, mata ki chowki, jagran or any family puja with a simple, devotional card.
puja.article:
Why families hold a puja and invite others

Many families hold a puja to give thanks for a blessing, to mark a new beginning or simply to bring the family together in devotion. The Satyanarayan katha is one of the most popular, often done on Purnima, after a wedding, on a birthday or when moving into a new home. A havan is performed for peace and purification. In North India, a jagran or mata ki chowki fills the night with bhajans for the Goddess, and a Sunderkand path is common on Tuesdays and Saturdays. Gujarati families often invite relatives for a Satyanarayan ni katha, a Ramdev Pir no path or a bhajan sandhya.

Whatever the puja, inviting people to share prasad and prayers is part of the joy. A simple card makes sure everyone knows the time the katha begins and when the aarti will be.

What to include

  • A devotional line at the top, like "|| Om Namo Narayanaya ||", "|| Jai Mata Di ||" or "|| Shri Ganeshaya Namah ||".
  • Name of the puja, such as Satyanarayan Katha, Havan, Mata ki Chowki or Sunderkand Path.
  • Occasion, if any, like "On the occasion of our son's birthday" or "On Kartik Purnima".
  • Date, day and time, with aarti and prasad timings.
  • Venue with a clear address.
  • Hosts and a contact number.

Traditional versus modern wording

Traditional

"With the grace of Lord Satyanarayan, we are organising a katha at our home. We humbly request you to attend with your family, take part in the aarti and accept prasad." This is the most common style for puja invitations.

Simple and friendly

"We are having a small Satyanarayan katha at home this Sunday. Do come for the aarti and prasad!" For neighbours and friends, a warm, simple line is enough.

Sample formats

Katha: || Om Namo Narayanaya || Satyanarayan Katha. On the occasion of Purnima. Sunday, 22 November 2026, katha at 5:00 PM, aarti at 6:30 PM, followed by prasad. At our home, A-12, Shivam Society, Rajkot. With best compliments from the Trivedi family.

Jagran: || Jai Mata Di || Mata ka Jagran. Saturday, 5 December 2026, from 9:00 PM till the Goddess's blessings. Community Park, Rohini, Delhi. Organised by the Gupta family.

When to send and reminders

For a small home puja, sending the card five to seven days ahead is enough. For a larger jagran or havan, send it about two weeks before. A reminder on the day, especially one mentioning the aarti time, helps guests who are coming only for the aarti and prasad. After the puja, a short thank-you message along with a photo of the decorated mandap is appreciated.

Etiquette for puja invitations

Puja invitations are usually open-hearted, and neighbours are always welcome. Mention whether a full meal will be served or only prasad, so guests can plan. If the puja is on a fasting day, it is thoughtful to note that the prasad is falahari. For an all-night jagran, give the approximate time of the main aarti and bhandara. Remind guests gently to dress modestly and to remove footwear outside the puja area, if the venue is a temple or home.

Many elders like to be personally invited for a puja, so a phone call along with the card is a respectful touch. If a pandit ji or bhajan mandali is coming from outside, share the same card with them so the timings match.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • No aarti time: many guests come only for the aarti and prasad. Give that time clearly.
  • Wrong day for the tithi: tithis sometimes change in the middle of the day. Confirm the date with the pandit ji before sending the card.
  • Not mentioning the meal: say whether it is prasad only or a full bhojan.
  • Missing contact number: for a jagran in a park or hall, give one number guests can call.

A message to send along with the card

For elders: "Jai Shri Krishna Foi, we are having a Satyanarayan katha at home on Purnima, 22 November, at 5 PM. Please come for the aarti and prasad. Card attached." For neighbours: "Katha at our home this Sunday evening, all are welcome for aarti at 6:30." The list below has more messages for every kind of puja.

Different pujas, different details

A havan usually needs guests to arrive before the purnahuti, so mention that time. A jagran goes on late into the night, so tell guests when the main aarti and bhandara will be. For a Sunderkand or Hanuman Chalisa path, the start time matters most because it is recited together. For a Ganesh sthapana during Ganesh Chaturthi, mention the days on which darshan is open and when the visarjan will be.

A clear card saves the host many phone calls on the day, leaving more time for the puja itself.

How to make a puja card on this site

  1. Enter the occasion or puja name, such as "On the occasion of Purnima".
  2. Add the date, time and venue.
  3. Enter the host family's names.
  4. Choose a devotional invitation line or write your own.
  5. Use the note for aarti time, prasad or bhandara details.
  6. Download and share the card on WhatsApp.

The heading on the card reads "Satyanarayan Katha" by default. You can adjust the wording to suit a havan, jagran, chowki or path. May the puja bring peace and blessings to your home.

faq.q: When is Satyanarayan katha usually done?
faq.a: It is often done on Purnima, and also on occasions like a wedding, birthday, griha pravesh, new job or any happy event in the family.

faq.q: Can I use this card for a havan or jagran?
faq.a: Yes. Change the wording and the occasion line to mention havan, jagran, mata ki chowki, Sunderkand path or any other puja.

faq.q: What should I write on a puja invitation?
faq.a: A devotional line at the top, the name of the puja, the occasion if any, date, time, aarti and prasad timing, venue and the host family's name.

faq.q: How early should I send a puja invitation?
faq.a: Five to seven days ahead for a home puja and about two weeks for a larger jagran or havan, with a reminder on the day.

faq.q: Should I mention whether a meal will be served?
faq.a: Yes, it helps guests plan. Write Prasad after aarti or Bhojan prasad to follow, as the case may be.

faq.q: Is it okay to invite neighbours on WhatsApp for a puja?
faq.a: Yes. Puja invitations are usually open to neighbours and friends, and a WhatsApp card is perfectly acceptable. Elders may appreciate a phone call as well.

shop-opening.h1: Shop and Office Opening Invitation Maker
shop-opening.sub: Announce your new shop, showroom, clinic or office and invite family, friends and customers to the muhurat and grand opening.
shop-opening.article:
A new business begins with blessings

Opening a new shop, showroom, clinic or office is a proud moment for any family. In Gujarat and North India, the opening is almost always done on a shubh muhurat, often on days like Dhanteras, Labh Pancham, Akshaya Tritiya, Vijayadashami or any date suggested by the family priest. The day usually starts with a Ganesh and Lakshmi puja, sometimes a Satyanarayan katha or a havan, followed by the ribbon cutting and the first sale, called the bohni in many families.

An invitation card for the opening does two things. It invites relatives and friends to share the joy, and it also serves as the first announcement of your business to potential customers. So the card should be both auspicious and clear.

What to include

  • A blessing line, such as "|| Shree Ganeshaya Namah ||" or "|| Shubh Labh ||".
  • Business name in full, exactly as on the signboard.
  • Type of business, if helpful, like "Jewellers", "Mobile Store" or "Dental Clinic".
  • Date and muhurat time of the opening and puja.
  • Full address with a landmark.
  • Owner or proprietor names, and the family.
  • A note about the chief guest, opening offers or a contact number.

Traditional versus modern wording

Traditional

"With the blessings of Lord Ganesh and Maa Lakshmi, we are starting our new venture. We cordially invite you to the muhurat and opening ceremony and request your good wishes." This suits relatives, elders and long-time business contacts.

Modern

"Something new is opening in town! Join us for the grand launch and be among our very first customers." This works well for friends, social media and customers.

Sample format

|| Shubh Labh ||

Grand Opening. Shree Krishna Jewellers. Muhurat on Monday, 9 November 2026 (Dhanteras) at 10:30 AM. Address: Shop No. 5, Ratnam Complex, C.G. Road, Ahmedabad. With best compliments from Shri Bharat Soni and family.

When to send and reminders

Send the invitation to relatives and close friends about one week before the opening. For customers and the wider public, share the card and a short message a few days before, and again on the day with the time and location. A reminder message on the morning of the opening is helpful. After the event, a thank-you message to everyone who came, with a photo of the opening, helps build goodwill for your business.

Etiquette and practical tips

Invite your neighbouring shopkeepers and building members. Their goodwill matters a lot in the long run. If you have a chief guest, confirm with them before printing their name. Mention if sweets or refreshments will be served. Keep the business name spelling consistent with your signboard and GST documents. Avoid overcrowding the card with too many offers; one clear line is enough.

If the puja is only for family and the public opening is later in the day, make two versions of the card with the right timings. For offices, you can mention "Office warming" or "Inauguration" instead of "Grand Opening".

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Different name spellings: the card, signboard and social media should all use the same spelling.
  • No landmark: new shops are hard to find. Add a landmark and send a location pin.
  • Unconfirmed chief guest: never print a name before they have agreed to come.
  • Too many offers: one clear offer line is better than a crowded card.

A message to send along with the card

For relatives: "Jai Shri Krishna Kaka, with the blessings of the family, I am opening my jewellery shop on Dhanteras. Muhurat is at 10:30 AM. Please come and do the first bohni for me. Card attached." For customers: "Shree Krishna Jewellers opens on Dhanteras at C.G. Road. Visit us for special opening offers!" More messages are in the list below.

After the opening

The days after the opening are important for any new business. Share photos of the puja and the ribbon cutting with a thank-you message, and save the numbers of guests who came. A short festive greeting from your shop on Diwali or New Year keeps you in their minds. You can make such greeting cards on this site as well, with your shop name printed on them.

If the opening falls near a festival, you can mention it on the card, for example "On the auspicious occasion of Labh Pancham". It adds warmth and makes the date easy to remember.

For an office, clinic or factory, the same card works well for a small inauguration. Invite your staff, suppliers and a few old clients along with the family, and keep the tone a little more formal. A simple line such as "We look forward to your continued support" is appreciated by business contacts.

How to make the card on this site

  1. Enter the shop or office name.
  2. Add the date and muhurat time.
  3. Type the full address with landmark as the venue.
  4. Add the owner or family names.
  5. Pick an invitation line or write your own.
  6. Use the note for chief guest, offers or contact number, then download and share.

We wish your new venture shubh labh, growth and success.

faq.q: What is a muhurat for a shop opening?
faq.a: A muhurat is an auspicious time chosen from the panchang or by a priest for starting the business. Many shops open on days like Dhanteras, Labh Pancham, Akshaya Tritiya or Dussehra.

faq.q: What should be written on a shop opening card?
faq.a: A blessing line, the business name, date and muhurat time, full address with landmark, owner names, and an optional note about the chief guest or offers.

faq.q: What is bohni?
faq.a: Bohni is the first sale of the day or of a new shop. It is considered auspicious, and families often ask a relative or respected guest to make the first purchase.

faq.q: Can I use this card for an office or clinic opening?
faq.a: Yes. Enter the office or clinic name and adjust the wording. The card works for any business inauguration.

faq.q: How early should I send the opening invitation?
faq.a: About a week before for relatives and friends, with a reminder on the morning of the opening. Share with customers a few days before and again on the day.

faq.q: Should I mention a chief guest on the card?
faq.a: Only after the chief guest has confirmed. Add their name in the note line.
